common_name: Chantilly Bearded Iris (Ruffled Pink Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Chantilly is a historically important mid-twentieth-century tall bearded iris prized for its soft pink coloring and heavily textured, ruffled form.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally just at or slightly above the soil surface in full sun with sharp drainage, since standing moisture around the rhizome invites rot. Chantilly carries soft, blended pink standards and falls with a notably ruffled, lace-like texture along the petal edges, a trait that was considered unusually refined when it was introduced and that influenced many later ruffled pink iris breeding lines. Its flowers have a delicate, almost translucent quality in bright sun. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom and discard the older, spent center sections, replanting only vigorous young rhizomes from the outer edge of the clump.

common_name: Argus Pheasant Bearded Iris (Classic Brown Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Argus Pheasant is an early-twentieth-century tall bearded iris grown for its bronze-and-cream plicata stitching pattern.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to sunlight in loose, well-drained soil, since bearded iris rot quickly if buried or kept wet. Argus Pheasant displays a cream to golden-tan ground stippled and stitched with rich brown-bronze marbling around the petal margins, a plicata pattern that was considered strikingly bold for its era and that helped popularize brown-toned iris breeding. The effect is strongest in cool spring weather and can soften somewhat in intense heat. Lift and divide clumps every three to four years once bloom declines, replanting only firm, disease-free rhizomes with a healthy fan of leaves attached.

common_name: Swan Ballet Bearded Iris (Vintage White Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Swan Ballet is a mid-twentieth-century white tall bearded iris noted for the graceful, flaring form of its blooms.

directions: Set rhizomes with their tops exposed at or just above soil level in a sunny bed with excellent drainage. Swan Ballet produces pure white flowers with wide, gracefully flaring falls and a softly ruffled edge, giving each bloom an airy, open look that reads as almost luminous against darker companion plantings. It was long admired among white iris for the elegant, flowing carriage of its blooms rather than for heavy ruffling or size. Keep plantings on the dry side through summer dormancy and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Solid Mahogany Bearded Iris (Deep Red-Brown Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Solid Mahogany is a Schreiner's-bred tall bearded iris valued for its deep, uniform red-brown coloring.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally with the tops exposed to full sun in a well-drained bed, as excess moisture around the crown leads quickly to bacterial soft rot. Solid Mahogany carries a rich, even red-brown self color across both standards and falls without the contrasting veining or shading seen in many brown-toned iris, giving the flower an unusually solid, velvety appearance. The deep tone pairs well with gold or copper companion plantings and reads as nearly black in low light. Divide every three to four years after bloom to prevent overcrowding, which can reduce flower count in subsequent seasons.

common_name: Mary Frances Bearded Iris (Orchid Blue-Pink Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Mary Frances is a widely grown tall bearded iris known for its soft orchid-blue coloring and ruffled form.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to sunlight in loose, well-drained soil. Mary Frances bears a soft, luminous orchid-blue tone that can shift toward lavender-pink depending on light conditions, with gently ruffled edges and a pleasant, light fragrance. Its unusual blended coloring made it a long-standing favorite for borders where a cooler-toned iris is wanted among warmer pastel companions. Lift and divide congested clumps every three to four years, keeping only vigorous young rhizomes from the outer rim for replanting.

common_name: Templecloud Bearded Iris (Vintage Blue-and-Pink Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Templecloud is a historically significant mid-twentieth-century tall bearded iris with soft blue-and-pink blended coloring.

directions: Plant rhizomes with tops exposed at or just above soil level in full sun with sharp drainage. Templecloud blends soft powder-blue standards with gently pink-toned falls, a muted, cloudlike color combination that was distinctive among iris of its era and that remains appealing in cottage-style plantings. The overall effect is soft and atmospheric rather than bold or high-contrast. Divide clumps every three to four years once flowering tapers off, replanting firm, disease-free rhizomes promptly so they can reestablish roots before winter.

common_name: Hello Darkness Bearded Iris (Deep Black-Purple Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Hello Darkness is a Schreiner's-bred tall bearded iris prized for its near-black, velvety flowers.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, avoiding low spots where water collects. Hello Darkness carries deep purple-black standards and falls with a velvety sheen that reads as nearly black in bright sun, offering strong contrast when paired with pale or silver-foliaged companions. The rich, saturated color intensifies in cooler spring weather and can look almost blue-black at dusk. Divide every three to four years to keep clumps vigorous, since overcrowded rhizomes produce fewer and smaller blooms over time.

common_name: Code of Honor Bearded Iris (White Iris with Red Beard)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Code of Honor is a Schreiner's-bred tall bearded iris with crisp white flowers and a bold red-orange beard.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in a sunny, well-drained bed, since bearded iris rhizomes need good air circulation around the crown to avoid rot. Code of Honor bears crisp white standards and falls set off by a vivid red-orange beard, a sharp color contrast that makes the flower stand out even from a distance in mixed borders. The clean white ground shows almost no veining, keeping the overall look crisp rather than blended. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom and replant healthy rhizomes promptly to let them establish before frost.

common_name: Classic Look Bearded Iris (White Plicata Edged in Blue)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Classic Look is a Schreiner's-bred tall bearded iris with a crisp white ground banded in clear blue.

directions: Set rhizomes with tops exposed at soil level in full sun with sharp drainage. Classic Look shows a clean white ground edged in a clear, even band of blue along the margins of the standards and falls, a tidy plicata pattern that gives the bloom a crisp, tailored appearance rather than the heavier stippling seen in older plicata types. The contrast holds up well from a distance, making it a strong choice for mass plantings. Lift and divide every three to four years once bloom declines to keep clumps healthy and floriferous.

common_name: Tiger Honey Bearded Iris (Golden Tan Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Tiger Honey is a modern tall bearded iris bred by Paul Black with warm golden-tan coloring.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally with the tops exposed to sunlight in loose, well-drained soil. Tiger Honey carries warm golden-tan standards over slightly deeper honey-gold falls, with fine veining near the beard that adds subtle texture without muddying the overall warm tone. The rich, sunny coloring makes it a strong companion for bronze or copper foliage plants in a border. Divide clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the oldest central rhizomes and replanting only vigorous outer divisions.

common_name: Decadence Bearded Iris (Ruffled Lavender-and-Gold Bicolor Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Decadence is a modern tall bearded iris with heavily ruffled lavender-and-gold bicolor flowers.

directions: Set rhizomes with tops exposed at or just above soil level in a sunny, well-drained bed. Decadence pairs soft lavender standards with warm gold-toned falls, both heavily ruffled along the edges, producing a lush, full-bodied bloom that looks especially striking in mass plantings. The combination of cool and warm tones on a single flower gives it unusual versatility when paired with other border perennials. Divide every three to four years once clumps become crowded, replanting healthy rhizomes right away so roots can establish before winter dormancy.

common_name: Blatant Bearded Iris (Bold Red-Violet Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Blatant is a tall bearded iris bred by Keith Keppel known for its vivid red-violet color.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed in full sun and well-drained soil, keeping the crown free of mulch that holds moisture. Blatant produces a saturated, uniform red-violet self with a matching beard, a bold, high-saturation color that lives up to its name and holds its intensity well even in strong sun. Its strong, upright stems carry well-branched flowers that make effective cut blooms as well as garden display. Lift and divide congested clumps every three to four years, replanting vigorous young rhizomes to maintain strong annual bloom.
